title: Replication: copies, leaders, and lag
story:
One copy of the data is one machine's worth of reads, one machine's worth of failure, and one location's worth of distance from everybody who is not near it. Replication answers all three at once, which is why it is nearly universal, and it introduces exactly one new problem that no amount of engineering removes.

The shapes are worth naming. A leader takes writes and followers receive them and serve reads — simple, because there is one place where order is decided, and limited, because that place is a single writer and a single failure. Or several peers each accept writes, which removes the single point and requires deciding what to do when two of them accepted conflicting ones.

The 2007 design is the clearest instance of the second because it states its motivation. The system replicates across nodes and maintains consistency among replicas during updates by a quorum-like technique together with a decentralised replica synchronisation protocol, using object versioning so that divergent copies can be detected, and pushing conflict resolution to the application where the system cannot decide. The motivation given is availability rather than performance: it exists to provide an always-on experience for core services, and sacrifices consistency under certain failure scenarios to get it. The stated consequence is that reads may return divergent versions which the application is expected to reconcile.

Read that last sentence as the design being honest rather than as a defect. The alternative to returning a divergent version is refusing to answer, and for the workload in question refusing is worse.

The new problem is lag. Between the moment a write is accepted and the moment it has reached every copy, the copies disagree, and a reader served by one that has not caught up is served an older state — one that may be older than a state that reader itself already observed. Shortening the window is possible. Closing it is not, because the copies are in different places and information takes time to travel, which is the same physical fact the latency lesson rested on.

So the engineering question is never whether to have lag but where to put it. Send reads that must see their own writes to the leader, or route a session consistently to one replica, or accept staleness explicitly for the reads that tolerate it — a follower count, a cached profile, a dashboard. What you must not do is leave it unspecified, because then every read is a coin toss whose bias changes with load.

problem.name: Replica divergence
problem.shape: One copy of the data limits reads, survives nothing, and sits far from most of its readers.
tell: a value written a moment ago reads back as its previous state
reads were moved to replicas to relieve the primary
a user sees their own change disappear on refresh
staleness tolerance has never been stated per read path
problem.move: Decide per read path how much staleness is acceptable, and route accordingly: reads that must observe their own writes go to the leader or to a pinned replica, and reads that tolerate lag are served anywhere and labelled as such. Measure the lag rather than assuming it, because it grows precisely when the system is busy.
problem.invariant: Between accepting a write and propagating it, copies disagree. The window can be shortened and cannot be closed, because the copies are in different places and information takes time to travel.
problem.breaks: Lag is largest exactly when it matters most. Replication falls behind under write load and during recovery, so the window widens during the incidents when users are most likely to be retrying and most likely to notice their own change missing.

cost.time: writes wait for however many copies you require before acknowledging, so stronger guarantees cost latency on every write
cost.space: a full copy of the data per replica
cost.beats: a single copy, which cannot scale reads, cannot survive a failure and cannot be near everyone

worked.problem: A value that was just written reads back stale. Is that a bug?
worked.reasoning:
It depends entirely on which read path served it, and the honest answer is that it is a bug only if nobody decided it was acceptable there.

The mechanism first. A write is accepted somewhere and then propagates to the other copies, and between those two moments the copies disagree. A read served by a copy that has not caught up returns the older state. Nothing has gone wrong in the sense of a malfunction — the system is doing what replication does.

Why the window cannot be closed is worth saying plainly, because people look for a setting that removes it. The copies are in different places and information takes time to travel, which is the same fact the latency lesson rested on. You can shorten the window by acknowledging writes only after more copies confirm, and you pay for that in write latency on every single write, forever. You cannot reduce it to zero while the copies remain in different places.

So the question is not whether lag exists but whether this particular read was allowed to see it. That is a design decision that should exist per read path. A user reloading the page after changing their own profile must see their change — that is read-your-writes, and violating it looks like data loss to the person it happens to, which is the worst possible impression. A follower count, a dashboard, a search index can be seconds behind and nobody is harmed.

The handling follows: route reads that must observe their own writes to the leader, or pin a session to one replica so it at least sees a consistent progression, or carry the write's version with the session and require a replica to have reached it. Reads that tolerate staleness go anywhere and should be labelled as tolerating it, so the next engineer does not have to guess.

The detail I would add unprompted is that lag is worst exactly when it matters most. Replication falls behind under heavy write load and during recovery, so the window widens during incidents — precisely when users are retrying, watching closely, and most likely to notice their own change missing. A system tested at low load will not show you this.

And the design instinct: the bug is rarely the staleness. It is that no one stated what each read path tolerates, so every read is a coin toss whose bias changes with load.

problem.practice: List your read paths and mark each one as must-see-own-writes or tolerates-lag. Then find one that is unmarked and serve it from a replica deliberately while making a change, and watch what a user would see. Separately, graph your replication lag against write volume.

beats.broke: One copy of the data is one machine's worth of reads, one machine's worth of failure, and one location's worth of distance from everybody who is not near it.
beats.fix: Keep several copies — a leader taking writes with followers serving reads, or several peers any of which accepts a write — so reads scale, failure is survivable, and data sits close to its readers.
beats.cost: Copies diverge between the moment of a write and the moment it arrives everywhere, so a reader can be served an older state than one already acknowledged — and no engineering removes that window, only shortens it.

interview.q: A value that was just written reads back stale. Is that a bug?
interview.trap: Answering yes and looking for a setting that eliminates it. The window cannot be closed while copies sit in different places — the real question is whether this particular read path was ever allowed to tolerate lag, and usually nobody decided.
